title: August and the Harvest
premise: Astrid Ashgrove is hired to appraise the Hollowell farmhouse, a property that seems to take inventory of her as she takes inventory of it. On the porch waits August, the imaginary friend she abandoned at age nine — unchanged, and now unmistakably real. As night falls, Astrid learns the house was built on a bargain: each generation must invite something in to keep the harvest coming, and her own childhood games were an invitation never rescinded. To survive until sunrise and free the generations of children bound inside its walls, Astrid must un-invite what she welcomed, name it before dawn, and accept that justice for the Hollowells will come from her memory, not any court.
about_author: Jonah Winterbourne is the pen name of a former rural land assessor who spent a decade cataloguing properties no one wanted to enter twice. He writes horror about houses, inheritance, and the debts families pretend aren't owed.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She arrives at the Hollowell farmhouse with clipboards and skepticism, measuring rooms that seem to measure back. Doors count wrong; a hallway is longer on the return. The beat is professional unease curdling into personal recognition.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. At dusk she finds August waiting on the porch, exactly as she left him at nine years old — same gap-toothed grin, same worn overalls. He says he kept the appointment. The emotional beat is vertigo: joy and terror in the same breath.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Things
chapters.summary: August's POV, rendered in his childlike cadence. He walks Astrid through the house he 'kept tidy' for thirty years, showing her toys arranged in rows and small doors she doesn't remember. The beat is tenderness laced with wrongness.

chapters.title: The Count Is Off
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She counts eleven doors upstairs, then twelve, then ten. In the twelfth doorway stands a girl in a 1950s dress who mouths help me before the wall seals over. The beat is dread: the house holds people, not secrets.

chapters.title: What Was Invited
chapters.summary: August's POV. He explains, without understanding, that Astrid invited him in with a rhyme from her childhood — and the house heard it too. Flashback threads show nine-year-old Astrid playing the game alone after her mother's death. The beat is grief reframed as culpability.

chapters.title: Mrs. Hollowell's Ledger
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In the cellar she finds a farmer's ledger where harvest yields are recorded beside children's names, one crossed out per good year. The last entry is her own surname. The beat is cold clarity: this is a contract, and she's collateral.

chapters.title: Sunset Clause
chapters.summary: August's POV. The sun goes down and the house exhales; walls breathe, floors tilt toward the kitchen like a throat. August shields Astrid, insisting he can keep the rules. The beat is protective love strained by his complicity.

chapters.title: The First Knock
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Something knocks from inside the walls, patient and rhythmic, matching her heartbeat. August warns her never to knock back. She almost does. The beat is temptation — the house offers warmth, family, belonging.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Dress
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The 1950s girl, Edie, reaches Astrid through a mirror, teaching her the house's grammar: it trades memories for hours of safety. Astrid pays with her mother's face. The beat is sacrifice and the first taste of real cost.

chapters.title: Harvest Supper
chapters.summary: August's POV. The kitchen sets itself for a feast of food that smells like every childhood summer. August eats; Astrid refuses. He begins to forget things — his own rhyme, his reason for waiting. The beat is heartbreak: obedience is erasure.

chapters.title: Midnight Census
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She finds the attic nursery where seven children sleep in beds that were never made, dreaming the house's dream. Edie's bed is empty and warm. The beat is horror sharpened into resolve: they can be woken.

chapters.title: The Bargain Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Edie's POV, sparse and old-fashioned. She recounts 1954: her father invited the thing in to save the farm from drought, and it took the children as interest. Every generation renewed it. The beat is inherited guilt and the question of who owes whom.

chapters.title: What August Kept
chapters.summary: August's POV. He reveals he isn't Astrid's invention — he was a Hollowell boy taken in 1971, given to her as a 'friend' so someone would eventually come back and open the door. The beat is devastating recontextualization: he was a message, not a memory.

chapters.title: Doors That Count
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Armed with the ledger, she maps the shifting rooms and realizes the extra door only exists between 3 and 4 a.m. — the hour of the original invitation. The beat is methodical hope: there is a mechanism, a way out.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: August's POV. The house turns openly hostile: hallways loop, the porch recedes, whispers use her mother's voice. August burns his stored memories to hold a corridor open. The beat is desperate loyalty at terrible price.

chapters.title: Edie's Crossing
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid wakes Edie by speaking her true name from the ledger, and Edie wakes screaming seventy years of held breath. One child freed means the house must collect another. The beat is triumph immediately taxed.

chapters.title: The Collection
chapters.summary: August's POV. The house comes for August as the lawful substitute. He accepts, asking only that Astrid remember him truly — not as imaginary, but as stolen. The beat is grief transformed into purpose.

chapters.title: Between Three and Four
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. In the impossible thirteenth hour, Astrid enters the extra door and finds the thing behind the house: vast, patient, wearing the shape of every parent who ever chose the farm over the child. The beat is confrontation with complicity itself.

chapters.title: Un-Invited
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, climax. She speaks the childhood rhyme backward, renouncing the invitation in her name and the Hollowells', naming the thing aloud so it can be refused. The house convulses; the nursery empties; August steps through the closing door into her arms. The beat is catharsis won at the edge of ruin.

chapters.title: Sunrise Appraisal
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Dawn finds the farmhouse ordinary, empty, worth nothing on paper. Astrid files a report declaring the property condemned — justice rendered outside any court. The beat is exhausted peace.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: August's POV, quiet coda. August, aging now like a real boy, plants a garden with Astrid and Edie on the ruined land. He asks if she'll forget him again; she says remembering is a chore you choose daily. The beat is found family, tender and watchful.

chapters.title: The Next Surveyor
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, final sting. Months later, a new surveyor knocks on Astrid's office door about a property 'that keeps counting.' Astrid closes the file, pockets the ledger's torn last page, and picks up her keys. The beat is vigilance: some invitations echo, and she intends to answer them first.
